Key Terms by Diagnosis Type

Core concepts, treatments, and exam patterns drawn from 900+ practice questions

Mood Disorders
Trauma / PTSD
EMDR Trauma-focused CBT Acute Stress Disorder Safety · Trustworthiness · Empowerment Crisis intervention DID / Dissociation Mandated reporting
  • Acute stress disorder = symptoms lasting 3 days – 1 month post-trauma; PTSD if beyond 1 month
  • Refer to support group only after the acute phase has subsided — groups are contraindicated acutely
  • Trauma-informed care: assume a trauma history; prioritize safety and accessibility for all clients
  • With rape/assault: address medical → emotional → legal concerns; first step is always physical exam
  • IPV with children present = mandated report even if children are not directly abused
  • DID hallmark: two or more distinct personality states + recurrent amnesia; treated with psychotherapy
  • For veterans with PTSD: EMDR + veterans' programs + family/parenting support is the comprehensive combo
  • Couples post-assault: establish explicit consent + trigger communication before resuming intimacy
Depression / MDD
Beck Depression Inventory-II Suicide risk assessment Hopelessness = strongest predictor 5150 / involuntary hold CBT Reminiscence therapy (elderly) Psychiatrist referral
  • Hopelessness is the single best predictor of suicide risk — flag it in every depressed client
  • Active suicide plan → initiate 5150 (involuntary hospitalization); safety contracts are insufficient alone
  • Other high-risk markers: prior attempt, giving away possessions, changing a will, access to lethal means
  • Children with MDD present with irritability, somatic complaints (stomachaches, headaches) rather than verbalizing sadness
  • Elderly depression: CBT + Reminiscence Therapy (life review) is evidence-based; EMDR not indicated without trauma
  • Client taking non-prescribed antidepressants → immediate psychiatric evaluation
  • Share test results in plain language; raw scores or jargon alone is unethical
  • Psychodynamic approach: explore unconscious roots and meaning of depression
Anxiety
CBT Exposure therapy ERP (OCD subtype) Rapport & safety first Social skills training Family systems approach
  • GAD = excessive worry across multiple domains for ≥ 6 months; Adjustment disorder = reaction to a specific stressor
  • For phobias: CBT with exposure is first-line; MFTs are generally trained and qualified to treat anxiety disorders
  • With anxious children: establish rapport and safety before any technique; work on social skills alongside anxiety
  • Family systems lens: anxiety often reflects family dynamic — address structure, not just the symptomatic individual
  • Separation anxiety + recent trauma: focus on trauma recovery first, then family/systemic work
Adjustment Disorder
Identifiable stressor Within 3 months of onset Subthreshold severity Short-term focus Specifiers: depressed / anxious / mixed
  • Diagnosis requires a clear psychosocial stressor and symptoms beginning within 3 months of its onset
  • Symptoms are clinically significant but do not meet full criteria for another disorder (e.g., MDD, PTSD)
  • Common on exam: new job loss, divorce, medical diagnosis, bereavement → short-term supportive + CBT
  • Specifiers matter: with depressed mood, with anxiety, with mixed emotional features, with disturbance of conduct
Bipolar Disorder
Mood stabilizers Psychiatrist collaboration 5150 for manic crisis Family psychoeducation Bipolar I vs II
  • Bipolar I: full manic episode required; Bipolar II: hypomania + major depressive episodes (no full mania)
  • Manic episode with poor judgment/impulse control → hospitalization is the priority
  • Suicidal with active plan + Bipolar I = 5150 immediately; medication + safety planning is insufficient
  • Client resists psychiatrist referral → explain the rationale clearly (medication management, not replacement of therapy)
  • Family members: psychoeducation on the disorder, cycles, and how to support without enabling
  • When in session and client acts out: call psychiatrist in the client's presence so both can hear the response
OCD
ERP (gold standard) Medication (SSRIs) Psychoeducation Ego-dystonic OCD + Anorexia comorbidity
  • Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) is the first-line treatment; combined with SSRIs for moderate–severe
  • OCD is ego-dystonic: obsessions feel intrusive and unwanted (vs. OCPD which is ego-syntonic)
  • Over 50% of anorexia nervosa clients meet OCD or social phobia criteria at some point — always screen
  • Psychoeducation for client and family is an important adjunct — helps reduce accommodation behaviors
Personality Disorders
Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD)
DBT (Linehan) Mindfulness Interpersonal effectiveness Distress tolerance Emotion regulation Splitting
  • Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) by Marsha Linehan is the evidence-based treatment specifically designed for BPD
  • DBT's four skill modules: mindfulness, interpersonal effectiveness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation
  • When client presents with extreme anger: let the client express emotions first before any redirection or technique
  • Splitting ("you're the best therapist ever" → "you're terrible") is a hallmark — remain consistent and non-reactive
  • Hospitalizations are common — always review discharge papers including toxicology reports on return to therapy
  • Therapeutic relationship with BPD clients is often ambivalent and confusing — this is diagnostic, not personal
Schizoid Personality Disorder
Social detachment Restricted affect No desire for closeness Cluster A
  • Pattern of detachment from social relationships and restricted range of emotional expression
  • Key distinction: person neither desires nor enjoys close relationships — this is not social anxiety (which involves wanting connection)
  • No close friends, solitary activities, indifferent to praise or criticism
Histrionic Personality Disorder
Attention-seeking Dramatic / exaggerated emotions Approval-seeking Cluster B
  • Constant seeking of approval and attention; overly reactive and dramatically expressed emotions
  • Relationships perceived as more intimate than they are; uses physical appearance to draw attention
  • Distinguished from BPD by the absence of self-harm, identity disturbance, and abandonment fears
OCPD
Perfectionism Inflexibility Need for control Ego-syntonic Cluster C
  • OCPD = persistent perfectionism, inflexibility, and need for control — the person sees these traits as reasonable
  • Ego-syntonic: the behaviors feel right and consistent with self (unlike OCD's intrusive, ego-dystonic obsessions)
  • Preoccupied with rules, orderliness, and schedules to the point that tasks are never finished
Paranoid Personality Disorder
Pervasive distrust Suspicion without evidence Misreads neutral actions Cluster A
  • Pervasive distrust and suspicion of others — reads neutral or benign actions as threatening or demeaning
  • Key exam clue: the word "suspicion" or "distrust" points strongly to paranoid PD (vs. schizoid = detachment)
  • Different from paranoid schizophrenia: no psychotic episodes, hallucinations, or disorganized thought
Sexual Disorders
Sexual Disorders & Sexual Concerns
Consent & trigger communication Sexual dysfunction Medical exam first Age-appropriate psychoeducation Paraphilias Substance use → sexual dysfunction
  • Post-assault couples: establish explicit consent + trigger communication before resuming intimacy — failure to do so risks re-traumatization
  • Alcohol and drug use are a primary cause of sexual dysfunction — always assess substance use in sexual complaints
  • Children showing sexual behaviors: assess for sexual abuse; look for age-inappropriate sexual knowledge, withdrawal, regression
  • Emotionally Focused Therapy (EFT) integrates attachment theory: insecure attachment → anxiety/avoidance patterns in intimacy
  • Age-appropriate psychoeducation: parents asking about children's sexual curiosity = normalize developmentally typical exploration
  • Sex offender treatment: highly structured; therapist must balance therapeutic relationship with community safety
Addiction & Substance Use
Eating Disorders
Anorexia vs. Bulimia Binge-Eating Disorder Narrative therapy (externalizing) OCD / anxiety comorbidity Denial → high dropout risk Weight restoration priority
  • Bulimia = binge + recurrent compensatory behaviors (purging, fasting, excessive exercise); Binge-Eating Disorder = binge without compensatory behaviors
  • Primary clue for bulimia vs. anorexia: client is not severely underweight but has loss of control over eating and compensatory behaviors
  • Over 50% of anorexia clients also meet criteria for OCD or social phobia — always screen for anxiety disorders
  • Narrative therapy technique: "How does the eating disorder affect you?" = externalizing — the disorder is separate from the person
  • Denial and lack of insight = highest dropout risk; motivational interviewing and alliance-building are essential
  • Medical stabilization and weight restoration must be addressed before purely psychological work in severe anorexia
Alcohol Use Disorder
Motivational Interviewing (MI) Al-Anon for family Generational patterns / codependency Direct confrontation Withdrawal risk
  • Motivational Interviewing (MI) is the client-centered approach for building readiness and commitment to change in ambivalent clients
  • When alcohol use is suspected but not confirmed: directly confront the client about the suspected use — avoidance is collusion
  • Family sessions: address generational patterns of alcoholism and codependency — systemic enabling must be named
  • Al-Anon: 12-step support group for family members and friends of people with alcohol problems
  • Court-mandated clients: address the alcohol use directly and therapeutically; mandated context doesn't mean only compliance is the goal
  • Elderly depression + alcohol use: treat both concurrently; address grief/loss and coordinate with the primary care physician
Heroin / Opioids
Buprenorphine (MAT) AB 816 — minors ≥ 16 Nar-Anon for family Flu-like withdrawal Therapeutic alliance = lifeline Grief / loss often underlying
  • Morphine / opioid withdrawal = flu-like symptoms: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle cramps, chills, runny nose, insomnia
  • AB 816 (effective Jan 1, 2024): minors 16 and older may consent to buprenorphine-based MAT outside a narcotic treatment program
  • Buprenorphine is a medication-assisted treatment (MAT) — do not discourage it; it is evidence-based and saves lives
  • The therapeutic alliance is often the primary support system — identify other people/services as protective factors
  • When a client is court-mandated for anger management but has opioid history: assess grief and loss first — substance use often masks underlying loss
  • Nar-Anon: 12-step support for family/friends of people using drugs (parallel to Al-Anon)
Stimulants (Cocaine, Meth, etc.)
Intoxication signs Nar-Anon for family Conduct disorder prerequisite (ASPD) Shared family goals first Antisocial comorbidity
  • Stimulant intoxication signs: dilated pupils, perspiration, agitation, confusion, increased talkativeness
  • Nar-Anon is to drug use what Al-Anon is to alcohol — support for families of drug-using individuals
  • ASPD diagnosis requires evidence of Conduct Disorder before age 15 — look for a history of early misconduct
  • When beginning family therapy with stimulant use: first define shared treatment goals with all family members before intervening
  • Stimulant use + aggression + extensive misconduct history → screen for Antisocial Personality Disorder
